title: Reformed consensus: justifying faith specially applies the Gospel — schools differ how
source_text: LXXIV. Porro ex iis quae fuerunt hactenus a nobis exposita facile videre est, ex communi quidem Reformatorum consensu, ad naturam fidei justificantis pertinere, ut generale Verbum Evangelii, & promissiones gratiae credenti cuique speciatim applicet. Sed tamen non omnes Scholae Reformatae Doctores applicationem istam eodem modo exponere & intelligere. Nam eorum multi sic loquuntur quasi per applicationem istam non aliud intelligerent, quam judicium illud quo fidelis statuit bona per Evangelium promissa & oblata peculiariter ad se pertinere, seque bonorum illorum & esse & fore compotem: Ut exempli gratia celeberrimus Petrus Molinaeus, Ursinus, Paraeus, & Daniel Tilenus.
pass_a_gloss: Further, from those things which have hitherto been set forth by us it is easy to see that, from the common consent of the Reformers, it pertains to the nature of justifying faith that it specially apply to each believer the general Word of the Gospel and the promises of grace. But yet not all Doctors of the Reformed School explain and understand that application in the same way. For many of them so speak as if by that application they understood nothing else than that judgment by which the believer lays down that the goods promised and offered through the Gospel pertain peculiarly to himself, and that he both is and will be partaker of those goods: as for example the most celebrated Peter du Moulin, Ursinus, Paraeus, and Daniel Tilenus.
pass_b_english: Common Reformed consent: justifying faith specially applies the general Gospel word and grace-promises to each believer.
Many reduce it to the judgment that Gospel goods are peculiarly mine, and that I am and will be partaker of them.
So du Moulin, Ursinus, Paraeus, and Tilenus.
